kernels.l1: Some cubbies get used and some stay empty. You can also ask who is in a cubby.
kernels.l2: The used arrowheads are the answers the machine can actually give. Tracing back from an arrowhead tells you which things get sent there — and sometimes nothing does.
kernels.l3: The image of a function is the set of answers it actually produces, which can be smaller than the codomain. The pre-image of a set is everything that lands in it, and it is allowed to be empty.
kernels.l4: The image is the set of values a function actually attains; the pre-image of a set is everything sent into it. The pre-image is defined for every function, and it may be empty.
kernels.l5: The image may be a proper subset of the codomain; the pre-image of a subset is defined for any function whatsoever, invertible or not.
kernels.l6: Image and pre-image are operations on subsets, not on elements. Tracing back is defined for every function, whether or not the function can be undone.
kernels.l7: The image is the set of values actually attained and may sit strictly inside the codomain. Tracing back is defined for every function and every target set, whether or not the function can be undone.
kernels.l8: The image is what a function actually produces; the pre-image is the set of inputs landing in a given target. Pulling back is the better-behaved direction, and §3.4 shows why.

kernel: Im(f) ⊆ T is the set of outputs actually hit. f⁻¹(U) is the set of inputs landing in U; it may be empty. f⁻¹({t}) ≠ ∅ exactly when t ∈ Im(f). Pre-images exist for any function, invertible or not.
objectives: Compute images and pre-images for given functions
